1:
The first question is what the cloths of service were. Gill reports Jarchi and Aben Ezra, who note that no linen is mentioned here and conclude that these were not the priestly vestments at all but the coverings thrown over the vessels of the sanctuary when the camp journeyed, though he adds that some take them for garments actually worn; Ellicott simply refers the phrase back to his note at Exodus 31:10. Henry and Wesley take the English words as a lesson rather than a problem: those who wear robes of honour must look on them as clothes of service, since from those on whom honour is put service is expected, and holy garments were not made for men to sleep in or to strut in but to do service in, and only so are they for glory and beauty. Both then read the vestments typologically — Christ as high priest putting on the clothes of service, arrayed with the gifts and graces of the Spirit which he received not by measure, bearing all God's spiritual Israel on his shoulders and in the breastplate of judgment, and crowning himself with holiness to the Lord; and believers as spiritual priests whose clean linen is the righteousness of saints.

Calvin defends the repetition itself. The description is more accurate than it would have been for an unimportant matter, and since Christ was vividly represented in the person of the high priest this was a most important part of the legal service. He is careful to say what it was not: not empty pomp, as when the Popish sacrificers dazzle the eyes of the simple with the splendour of their vestments to acquire dignity, but a means of placing before men's eyes everything faith ought to consider in Christ — the mitre inscribed Holiness to the Lord, the ephod bearing the symbols of the tribes so that in the person of one all might be presented familiarly before God. He counts the refrain as the Lord commanded Moses seven times over and says the repetition awakens attention; Henry counts six paragraphs closing that way and lists the verses, adding that no earlier account of the tabernacle's furniture carries the like, as though these garments in particular required both warrant and direction. Clarke, for his part, prefixes a bare table of contents for the chapter and refers the colours to his note at Exodus 25:4.

The gold thread divides Clarke and Ellicott. Both describe the same operation — gold beaten into thin plates and cut into wires to be worked with the coloured yarn — and draw opposite inferences from it. Ellicott calls the method very primitive, nowhere else mentioned, and says it implies a ruder state of metallurgy than we should have expected, adding that the coloured threads and the white linen were woven into a patterned fabric first and the gold inserted afterwards as embroidery, as in Egypt. Clarke refuses that inference: he cannot suppose the Israelites had not then the art of making gold thread, since they possessed several ornamental arts much more difficult, and suggests instead that the work in hand called for figures in a more solid form than gold thread could give. Gill supplies the rabbinic recipe the other two leave out — one thread of pure gold twisted with six of blue, another with six of purple, another with six of scarlet, another with six of linen, four threads of gold and twenty-eight threads in all.
6: Clarke ventures one identification and declines the rest. The onyx stones set in the shoulder-pieces are, he suggests, possibly the Egyptian pebble — offered as a possibility and not a decision, with the reader sent to Exodus 25:7 and Exodus 28:17 for the argument. The breastplate he treats as already described at Exodus 28:15, and the four rows of stones set in it as fully explained at the same place. Ellicott handles the shoulder-stones the same way, referring their character as a memorial for the children of Israel to his note at Exodus 28:12. Both men are working on the principle that this chapter is an execution report whose terms were fixed in the instructions, so that the exegetical weight belongs to chapter 28 and what stands here is the record that the thing was in fact done.
23:
Clarke explains the hole in the robe by a piece of medieval European armour. The habergeon, or hauberk, was a small coat of mail in the form of a half shirt, made of small iron rings curiously united together; it covered the neck and breast, was very light, and resisted the stroke of a sword, and sometimes went over the whole head as well. He then traces it eastwards rather than westwards: this kind of defensive armour was used among the Asiatics, particularly the ancient Persians, among whom it is still worn, and it seems to have been borrowed from them by the Norman crusaders. The comparison is offered for the shape of the opening — a neck-hole bound so that it should not tear — rather than for any likeness of material.

Ellicott corrects the rendering of the pomegranates. The Authorised words make the blue, the purple and the scarlet one thing and the twined linen another; the Hebrew, he says, means rather of blue, and purple, and scarlet, twisted together, so that the three colours are spun into a single thread and the linen is not a separate material at all. He compares the instruction at Exodus 28:33, and refers the question of what the golden bells between the pomegranates were for to his note at Exodus 28:35.
27:
Ellicott corrects the English at four points running, and every correction pulls in the same direction — away from the ecclesiastical colouring the Authorised words have acquired and back towards ordinary clothing. The coats are rather tunics or shirts; the mitre is rather a turban, and it was Aaron's alone; the goodly bonnets are rather caps, and they were for his sons; the linen breeches are rather linen drawers, and these were made both for Aaron and for his sons. Each correction is referred back to the corresponding instruction in chapter 28. He also notices something the chapter does that the earlier one did not: the girdle, which belonged to Aaron, is described here much more fully than in the instructions, where it is called simply a girdle of needlework — so the execution narrative is not everywhere a shorter echo of the command, but at this one point tells the reader more.

On the plate of the holy crown Ellicott again refers the reader to Exodus 29:6, while Clarke sets the object in comparative company. On Asiatic monuments, particularly those in the ruins of Persepolis, and on many Egyptian monuments, priests are represented wearing crowns or tiaras, and sometimes their heads are crowned with laurel; and Cuper observes that among the ancient Greeks priests and priestesses alike were styled crown-bearers, because they officiated with crowns sometimes of gold and sometimes of laurel upon their heads. The point is not that Israel borrowed the ornament but that a crowned head was what a priest looked like across the whole ancient world.
32:
Henry begins from the speed of the work. It was not much more than five months from beginning to finishing, and though there was a great deal of the sort of work that is usually the work of time — embroidering and engraving, not only in gold but in precious stones — they went through with it quickly and yet with the greatest exactness imaginable. He gives three reasons: many hands were employed, unanimous and not striving with each other; the workmen were taught of God and so were kept from making the blunders that would have retarded them; and the people were hearty and zealous, impatient till it was done, because God had prepared their hearts. Wesley carries the same account, the same five months and the same explanation from the workmen's teaching and the people's zeal.

What was brought to Moses, and why, occupies the rest. Gill notes that the several parts came before they were put together, and were examined in the order in which they had been commanded, so that Moses might see whether the pattern shown him had been followed. Henry presses the submission itself: the workmen did not object that Moses was no judge of such work, but the God who gave them knowledge to do it gave them humility to have it examined; the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets; and in any case Moses had the more exact idea of the model, so that they could not be satisfied with their own work until he had approved it. On the exactness Henry draws the analogy out — all the copies of God's grace agree with the original of his counsels, and when the mystery of God is finished not one iota of his purpose will be found to have fallen to the ground. Clarke refers the whole to the command at Exodus 25:40 and observes that Moses repeated everything in the most circumstantial detail precisely to show that he had conscientiously observed the directions he received. Calvin reads the summary as a guarantee of purity: it declares that in no part was there the least defect, whence we gather that no part of the building was impaired by any admixture.

The blessing divides them. Henry takes it in two parts — Moses commended them, and did not find fault where there was none, as those do who think they disparage their own judgement unless they can find something amiss in the best performance; and he prayed for them, blessing them as one having authority, since the less is blessed of the better. There is no record of wages, and Henry gives three reasons why none were owing: they wrought for themselves, they had their meat from heaven and their raiment did not wear out, and the blessing itself was wages enough. Calvin denies that it was a prayer at all in the ordinary sense. It was not a simple petition such as a private individual makes, but a promise of reward, calculated to awaken confidence in the people when they heard from the mouth of so excellent and unimpeachable a witness that their labour was pleasing to God. Keil looks past the blessing to the inventory, noting that the shewbread, the oil for the candlestick and for anointing, and the fragrant incense were delivered along with the vessels, so that everything required for the daily worship was in hand and the service could begin the moment the tabernacle was set up. Ellicott adds only that the vail here listed is the one that divided the holy place from the most holy, covering the latter from the sight of man.
37:
The inventory has reached the candlestick, and the one clause in it that is not a bare name divides Clarke from Ellicott. The Authorised words are the lamps to be set in order, and the two men construe them in incompatible ways.

Clarke reads the phrase as an action, and a recurring one. The lamps were to be trimmed and freshly oiled every day, for the purpose of being lighted in the evening; the setting in order is the daily service of the priest, and he sends the reader to Exodus 27:21, the standing ordinance that the lamp be tended from evening to morning. On that construal the clause is not really describing the object at all but attaching to it the duty that will follow once it is in use. The candlestick itself he does not describe again, referring it to his note at Exodus 25:31.

Ellicott reads the phrase as a description of position. The Hebrew, he says, is the lamps of arrangement — a noun, not a task — and the reference is probably to the arrangement of the lamps in a single line or row upon the candlestick. His comparison is with Leviticus 24:6, where the shewbread is set out in rows on the pure table, so that the same kind of expression governs a spatial disposition rather than an act of maintenance. The difference matters for what the verse is doing here: on Ellicott's reading the clause tells the reader how the finished object looked when it was carried in and laid before Moses, which is what an inventory of delivered work would naturally record; on Clarke's it looks past the delivery to the ministry the lamps were made for.

Keil, working through the same list, glosses only one term in it. Against all the vessels of the service of the tabernacle he sets a cross-reference to Exodus 27:19, where the phrase was defined, and then carries the narrative to its close: when Moses had received and examined all the different articles, and found that everything was made according to the directions of Jehovah, he blessed the children of Israel.
41:
The last line of the inventory turns on a conjunction that is not there. The Authorised Version reads the cloths of service to do service in the holy place, and the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and his sons' garments, which makes three classes of thing handed over. Ellicott points out that there is no and in the original, and would translate: the cloths of service to do service in the holy place — the holy garments for Aaron the priest, and his sons' garments. On that punctuation the second and third clauses are exegetical of the first: cloths of service is not a separate class of fabric standing beside the priestly vestments but the general heading under which those vestments are listed, and the verse names one thing and then says what it consists of.

The reading has consequences beyond this verse, and Ellicott makes them explicit by sending the reader to the same note at Exodus 31:10 that he cited for the identical phrase at the head of the chapter. His construal is therefore the same at both ends of it: whatever the cloths of service were at the beginning, they are here identified with the garments of Aaron and his sons, and the chapter closes its list with the same term it opened with.

Keil is not interested in the grammar and takes the verse as the hinge into what follows. When Moses had received and examined all the different articles, and found that everything was made according to the directions of Jehovah, he blessed the children of Israel. The ground Keil gives for that blessing is not the quality of the workmanship but the temper of the people: the readiness and liberality with which they had presented the gifts the work required, and the zeal with which they had executed the whole of it in rather less than half a year — a figure he reckons from the date given at Exodus 40:17. Both were most cheering signs of Israel's willingness to serve the Lord, and for such willingness, he says, they could not fail to receive the blessing of God.
43:
What Moses did is agreed and quickly told. Gill has him make a survey of the whole, examining with great care and accuracy every particular thing and the manner in which it was finished; Wesley has him look at it piece by piece; Ellicott says he inspected it to see whether it was according to the pattern shown him, and being satisfied expressed his own approval and God's by blessing those who had worked so faithfully. Clarke adds the chain of command: Moses was the general superintendent of the whole, under whom Bezaleel and Aholiab were employed, and the other workmen under them, and it was Moses who had laid the pattern he received before them to work by. Gill puts the accuracy down to the workmen rather than the inspector — they were throughout filled by the Spirit of God with wisdom and understanding to do everything just as it was God's pleasure it should be done — and Wesley says the same in a sentence: the same who showed Moses the pattern guided their hand in the work.

What the blessing was is less settled. Clarke gives it two senses and prefers to hold both. In the first place Moses gave them the praise due to their skill, diligence and fidelity, and Clarke defends that sense of the word from his note at Genesis 2:3 and from the exchange between Boaz and his reapers at Ruth 2:4, which he calls a fine instance of ancient courtesy between masters and servants. But it is very probable, he adds, that Moses also prayed for them, that they might be prospered in all their undertakings and brought at last to the inheritance that fadeth not away. Wesley makes the same division sharper — Moses not only praised them but prayed for them, blessing them as one having authority — and then argues that no wages were owing: they wrought for themselves, the honour of God's tabernacle among them being recompense enough, and they had their meat from heaven at free cost and their raiment did not wear out, so that they neither needed wages nor had reason to expect any. Clarke and Wesley agree that the blessing extended past the artificers, Clarke because the people had contributed liberally and the workmen wrought faithfully so that the blessing was pronounced on all, Gill because it may be understood both of those who had given and of those who had built. Gill alone supplies a form of words, from the Targum of Jonathan and from Jarchi: may the divine Majesty of the Lord dwell in the works of your hands.

Clarke then takes the tabernacle for a type of the human nature of Christ — a shrine not made with hands, formed by God himself and worthy of the fullness of the Deity that dwelt in it — and rests the reading on John 1:14, where the Word made flesh is said to have pitched his tent among us, so that the disciples beheld his glory as Israel beheld the glory resting on the tabernacle. He presses the parallel to its purpose: the tent was raised that God might dwell among the children of Israel, and the human nature was produced that the Godhead might dwell in it and God and man be reconciled, which he closes by turning on the reader as a question about the indwelling of God in the soul.
